lede: An employee's manager is another row of the same table. A self join matches a table with itself, and a cross join goes the other way: it pairs every row with every row, which is how you build a complete grid.
objectives: Give two copies of one DataFrame different names with `alias`
Join a table to itself to look up a related row, such as a manager
Chain self joins to climb more than one level
Build every combination of two DataFrames with `crossJoin`, and predict its size

blocks.md:
In `employees`, `manager_id` holds the `employee_id` of the person's manager. To show each employee next to their manager's name, join `employees` with itself: one copy plays the employee, the other the manager.

Both copies have the same column names, so give each a name with `alias`. `employees.alias("e")` is the same data, but now its columns can be written `F.col("e.first_name")`, and the other copy's `F.col("m.first_name")`.

blocks.title: Each employee and their manager
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

e = employees.alias("e")
m = employees.alias("m")

pairs = e.join(m, F.col("e.manager_id") == F.col("m.employee_id"), "left")

pairs.select(
    "e.employee_id",
    "e.first_name",
    "e.job_title",
    F.col("m.first_name").alias("manager"),
    F.col("m.job_title").alias("manager_title"),
).orderBy("e.employee_id").show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: The chief executive has no manager. A left join keeps that row with NULLs; an inner join would drop it. The join condition decides which copy is which: `e.manager_id` matches `m.employee_id`.

blocks.md: After a self join every column name exists twice. Asking for a bare name doesn't say which copy you mean.

blocks.title: Which first_name?
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

e = employees.alias("e")
m = employees.alias("m")

pairs = e.join(m, F.col("e.manager_id") == F.col("m.employee_id"), "left")
pairs.select("employee_id", "first_name").show()
blocks.note: The message lists both candidates, `e`.`employee_id` and `m`.`employee_id`. Prefix every column with its alias and rename the manager's columns with `.alias(...)` so the result has unique names.

blocks.md: Each self join climbs one level. To reach the manager's manager, add a third copy and join it on the second copy's `manager_id`. An inner join here keeps only people who have both levels above them.

blocks.title: Two levels up
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

e = employees.alias("e")
m = employees.alias("m")
mm = employees.alias("mm")

chain = (
    e.join(m, F.col("e.manager_id") == F.col("m.employee_id"), "inner")
    .join(mm, F.col("m.manager_id") == F.col("mm.employee_id"), "inner")
)

chain.select(
    "e.employee_id",
    "e.first_name",
    F.col("m.first_name").alias("manager"),
    F.col("mm.first_name").alias("managers_manager"),
).orderBy("e.employee_id").show()
blocks.note: The two heads and the chief executive are gone: the heads' manager has no manager, and the chief executive has none at all. A fixed number of joins climbs a fixed number of levels.

blocks.md:
A **cross join** has no condition at all: every row on the left is paired with every row on the right. `a.crossJoin(b)` has `a.count() × b.count()` rows.

That's exactly what a planning grid needs: one row for every department in every quarter, so a department with nothing planned still gets a row to fill in.

blocks.title: A grid of departments and quarters
blocks.code:
quarters = spark.createDataFrame([("2026-Q1",), ("2026-Q2",), ("2026-Q3",), ("2026-Q4",)], "quarter STRING")

grid = departments.select("department_id", "department_name").crossJoin(quarters)
print(departments.count(), "x", quarters.count(), "=", grid.count())

grid.orderBy("department_id", "quarter").show()
blocks.note: 3 departments times 4 quarters gives 12 rows. The result has the columns of both sides.

blocks.title: Cross joins grow fast
blocks.note: Every employee paired with every employee, including themselves: 9 × 9 = 81. With 10,000 employees it would be 100 million rows. Cross join small tables on purpose, never large ones by accident.

concept.prompt: Why does a self join need `alias`?
choices: Spark can't join a DataFrame with itself any other way
Both copies have the same column names, so each copy needs a name to tell them apart
`alias` makes a physical copy of the data
concept.why: `alias` doesn't copy anything; it names each side so `F.col("e.first_name")` and `F.col("m.first_name")` mean different columns.

concept.prompt: The chief executive's `manager_id` is NULL. Is the chief executive in an inner self join of employees to managers?
choices: No: a NULL key matches nothing, so an inner join drops the row
concept.why: With no matching manager row the inner join drops it. Use a left join to keep everyone.

concept.prompt: `a` has 6 rows and `b` has 5. How many rows does `a.crossJoin(b)` have?
concept.why: A cross join pairs every row with every row: 6 × 5 = 30.

review: A self join matches a table with itself; `df.alias("x")` names each copy.
Refer to columns as `F.col("x.name")`, and rename one side's columns so the result has unique names.
The join condition decides the roles: `e.manager_id == m.employee_id` makes `m` the manager.
Use a left self join to keep rows with no match, such as the person at the top.
Each extra self join climbs one more level.
`a.crossJoin(b)` pairs every row with every row: `a.count() × b.count()` rows. Use it for small grids only.
